lesson.title: The Oil King: John D. Rockefeller and the Standard Oil Empire
lesson.summary: John D. Rockefeller built Standard Oil into the dominant force in the American oil industry through relentless horizontal integration, eventually controlling roughly ninety percent of the country's oil refining before the government broke his company apart.
lesson.body:
John D. Rockefeller was born in 1839 in Richford, New York, and grew up in a household shaped by a hardworking mother and an unreliable, often absent father. He began his career as a bookkeeper in Cleveland, Ohio, and by his early twenties had entered the oil refining business, drawn by the boom that followed the discovery of oil in western Pennsylvania in 1859. In 1870, Rockefeller and several partners founded the Standard Oil Company in Cleveland, entering an industry that at the time had dozens of small, competing refiners.

Rockefeller's central strategy was horizontal integration: rather than trying to control every stage of oil production the way Carnegie controlled steel, Rockefeller focused on dominating a single stage, refining, by buying out or driving out competing refineries until Standard Oil controlled the great majority of the market. He achieved this partly through genuine efficiency, running his refineries with careful attention to cost and waste, and partly through aggressive tactics, including secret deals with railroads for favorable shipping rates that competitors could not match, which made it very difficult for smaller refiners to survive.

By the early 1880s, Standard Oil controlled an estimated ninety percent or more of American oil refining capacity. To manage this sprawling empire, Rockefeller's lawyer Samuel Dodd helped design a new legal structure in 1882 called the Standard Oil Trust, in which stockholders of many formally separate companies handed their shares to a small board of trustees who then ran the entire network as one coordinated enterprise. This trust became the model, and the namesake, for the broader category of trusts that other industries soon copied.

Standard Oil's dominance made it the most famous target of the era's growing backlash against corporate power. Journalist Ida Tarbell, whose own father had been squeezed out by Standard Oil's tactics, published a detailed investigative history of the company starting in 1902 that exposed its methods to a national audience and became one of the defining works of muckraking journalism. Public pressure built alongside legal action, and in 1911 the United States Supreme Court ruled in Standard Oil Company of New Jersey versus United States that the company violated the Sherman Antitrust Act and ordered it broken into more than thirty separate companies, several of which, including predecessors of ExxonMobil and Chevron, remain familiar names today.

In his later years, Rockefeller devoted enormous resources to philanthropy, founding the University of Chicago and later the Rockefeller Foundation, which funded major advances in medicine and public health. He died in 1937, and by most historical estimates adjusted for the size of the American economy at the time, he remains the wealthiest individual in United States history, a legacy that, like Carnegie's, combines extraordinary business dominance with equally extraordinary philanthropic giving.
